lesson.title: Inferir vocabulário em contexto
lesson.objective: Inferir sentidos prováveis de palavras em inglês a partir de pistas explícitas, relações entre frases e função gramatical, testando a hipótese e reconhecendo ambiguidades.
lesson.summary: Leia o enunciado todo, identifique a pista, formule um sentido aproximado e confira se ele funciona na frase. Contexto ajuda, mas nem sempre determina uma tradução única.
lesson.explanation:
## 1. Leia a frase inteira primeiro
Observe a função da palavra: nomeia uma coisa, descreve, indica ação ou liga ideias? Evite parar na primeira semelhança com o português. Um cognato pode ajudar, mas não prova o significado.

## 2. Procure pistas próximas
Uma explicação depois de dois-pontos, exemplos após “such as”, uma consequência ou uma paráfrase podem restringir o sentido. Conectores como “because”, “unlike”, “but” e “in other words” mostram relações diferentes. Leia o trecho anterior e o seguinte quando necessário.

## 3. Teste a hipótese
Proponha um sinônimo simples e substitua a palavra na frase completa. A gramática e a lógica continuam coerentes? Compare com o que a frase diz explicitamente; não descarte uma evidência só porque ela contraria seu primeiro palpite.

## 4. Diferencie palavra polissêmica de pista suficiente
Uma palavra como “light” pode significar “leve” ou “claro”, dependendo da frase. A situação pode escolher um sentido. Em outras frases, como “the result was remarkable” sem descrição do resultado, o contexto informa que houve uma avaliação, mas não explica o motivo.

## 5. Informe o limite
Se dois sentidos ainda se encaixarem, não invente certeza. Consulte um dicionário apropriado ou mais texto e registre a ambiguidade até encontrar nova evidência. Inferência contextual produz uma leitura provável, não necessariamente uma tradução exata.
lesson.workedExample: Em “The path was muddy after the storm, so hikers chose a dry route”, “muddy” é desconhecida. “After the storm” e a escolha de uma rota “dry” apontam para umidade. Testando “covered with mud” na frase, a relação continua coerente. Essa é a hipótese mais apoiada; a frase não informa a profundidade da lama.
lesson.commonMistake: Escolher o primeiro significado do dicionário ou um falso cognato, sem testar a hipótese contra as pistas da frase inteira.
tips: Sublinhe a palavra-alvo e circule a pista textual.
Diga se a pista é causa, contraste, exemplo, consequência ou paráfrase.
Substitua por um sinônimo e mantenha a incerteza quando duas leituras couberem.
priorKnowledge: Localizar palavras frequentes em uma frase curta.
Reconhecer conectores comuns como because, but e such as.

progression.focus: Usar definições, causas, contrastes e exemplos explícitos.
Inferir palavras por consequência, forma, ação, exemplos e sentidos múltiplos.
Combinar pistas, interpretar modalização e reconhecer ambiguidade real.
Testar hipóteses e limitar conclusões à evidência do trecho.
Reaplicar o procedimento e consultar fontes quando o contexto não basta.

microExplanations.text: A causa e o efeito ajudam a limitar o sentido, mas não revelam detalhes que a frase não informa.
“Such as” introduz exemplos; “in other words” costuma reapresentar a ideia. Use a relação, não uma palavra isolada.
Uma palavra pode ter sentidos diferentes. Teste qual deles explica a ação ou situação descrita.
Troque a palavra por um sinônimo aproximado e confira gramática e coerência no enunciado completo.
Se duas leituras continuam possíveis, preserve a ambiguidade e procure mais evidência.

remediations.prompt: Copie a palavra desconhecida e marque as palavras da frase que dão uma definição, exemplo, causa, contraste ou consequência.
Proponha um sinônimo simples e leia a frase novamente. Explique qual parte continua coerente ou entra em conflito.

remediations.misconception: Usar sempre o primeiro sentido conhecido.
remediations.prompt: Liste dois sentidos possíveis e associe cada um a uma pista. Elimine apenas o que não combina com o contexto.

remediations.misconception: Tratar uma possibilidade como fato confirmado.
remediations.prompt: Complete: “O trecho apoia ___ porque ___. Ainda não informa ___.”
Indique quais dois sentidos ainda cabem e que frase, exemplo ou fonte ajudaria a distingui-los.

questions.statement: Read: “The jar is empty. There is no honey left.” What does “empty” mean here?
questions.correctAnswer: Containing nothing.
questions.explanation: The second sentence explains “empty”: no honey remains in the jar.
questions.hint: Use the clue “There is no honey left.”

questions.statement: Read: “Nina whispered because the baby was asleep.” What does “whispered” most likely mean?
questions.correctAnswer: Spoke very quietly.
questions.explanation: The sleeping baby gives a reason to use a quiet voice.
questions.hint: Connect the action to the reason introduced by “because.”

questions.statement: Read: “Unlike the rough path, the paved road was smooth.” Which meaning best fits “rough”?
questions.correctAnswer: Uneven or not smooth.
questions.explanation: “Unlike” marks a contrast: the paved road is smooth, while the other path is not.
questions.hint: Use the contrast with “smooth.”

questions.statement: Read: “The coach called Ravi reliable: he arrived on time each day.” What does “reliable” mean here?
options: Someone who can be depended on.
questions.correctAnswer: Someone who can be depended on.
questions.explanation: Arriving on time repeatedly is evidence that Ravi can be depended on.
questions.hint: The example after the colon explains the adjective.

questions.statement: Read: “The first room held only two desks. The next room was spacious, with tables for twenty learners.” What does “spacious” mean?
questions.correctAnswer: Having plenty of room.
questions.explanation: The contrast in capacity and the tables for twenty indicate that the second room has more space.
questions.hint: Compare the number of desks and tables.

questions.statement: A label says “FRAGILE”; the delivery note adds, “Handle gently: the glass inside can break.” What does “fragile” mean?
questions.correctAnswer: Easily broken or damaged.
questions.explanation: The note explicitly links the label to glass that can break.
questions.hint: Use the explanation after the semicolon.

questions.statement: Read: “After three dry months, clean water became scarce; the town opened an extra supply point.” What does “scarce” mean in this passage?
options: Limited and not easy to find.
questions.correctAnswer: Limited and not easy to find.
questions.explanation: The dry period and extra supply point indicate limited availability.
questions.hint: Ask why the town opened another supply point.

questions.statement: Read: “Leila was reluctant to present. She paused at the doorway and asked whether a partner could begin.” What does “reluctant” suggest?
options: She had already completed the presentation.
She was certain the room was empty.
She wanted to speak first without help.
She was hesitant or not eager to begin.
questions.correctAnswer: She was hesitant or not eager to begin.
questions.explanation: Pausing and asking a partner to begin are clues of hesitation, though they do not tell us exactly why.
questions.hint: Use the actions as evidence and avoid guessing her reason.

questions.statement: Read: “The forest was dense; only a narrow trail passed between the closely spaced trees.” What does “dense” mean?
options: Being located far from a town.
questions.correctAnswer: Having many trees close together.
questions.explanation: “Closely spaced trees” directly explains the relevant sense of “dense.”
questions.hint: Look for the phrase that describes distance between the trees.

questions.statement: Read: “Mateo showed generosity by sharing his supplies with classmates who had none.” What does “generosity” mean in this context?
options: A plan to collect every supply.
A willingness to give or share with others.
A rule that everyone must work alone.
A skill for repairing broken items.
questions.correctAnswer: A willingness to give or share with others.
questions.explanation: Sharing supplies with people who have none is an example of giving to others.
questions.hint: Use the action after “by” as an example.

questions.statement: Read: “The guide is useful because it gives clear steps that help new visitors.” What does “useful” mean?
options: Written in a language no one knows.
questions.correctAnswer: Helpful for a purpose.
questions.explanation: The clear steps help visitors, so the guide serves a helpful purpose.
questions.hint: The clause after “because” states the benefit.

questions.statement: Read: “The bag is light, so Jo carried it upstairs without stopping.” Which meaning of “light” fits?
questions.correctAnswer: Not heavy.
questions.explanation: Carrying the bag upstairs without stopping supports the weight meaning.
questions.hint: Choose the sense that explains the action.

questions.statement: Read: “The train was delayed, but it eventually arrived at 8:10.” What does “eventually” mean here?
options: In the end, after some delay.
questions.correctAnswer: In the end, after some delay.
questions.explanation: The delay followed by arrival shows that the event happened in the end.
questions.hint: Compare “was delayed” with “arrived.”

questions.statement: Read: “The recipe uses herbs, such as basil and parsley, for flavor.” Which meaning of “herbs” is supported?
options: Any object used to measure heat.
Plants used here to add flavor to food.
A method for freezing a recipe.
questions.correctAnswer: Plants used here to add flavor to food.
questions.explanation: Basil and parsley are examples, and the sentence states their purpose.
questions.hint: Use both the examples and the phrase “for flavor.”

questions.statement: Read: “The river current was strong after the rain, so the team waited before crossing.” What does “current” mean?
questions.correctAnswer: The flow of water.
questions.explanation: The river and crossing context point to moving water.
questions.hint: Check which meaning fits both “river” and “crossing.”

questions.statement: A report says: “The new shade may reduce room temperature; measurements will continue for two weeks.” Which interpretation matches the evidence?
options: The room is already cooler in every measurement.
Two weeks of results have already been collected.
A reduction is possible, but it has not yet been confirmed.
questions.correctAnswer: A reduction is possible, but it has not yet been confirmed.
questions.explanation: “May” indicates possibility, and future measurements show the claim remains under investigation.
questions.hint: Keep certainty at the level expressed by “may.”

questions.statement: Read: “After reviewing the schedule, the applicant withdrew the request. In other words, the request was no longer being pursued.” What does “withdrew” mean?
options: Formally took back or stopped pursuing the request.
Moved the request to a higher shelf.
Asked for the request to be approved immediately.
questions.correctAnswer: Formally took back or stopped pursuing the request.
questions.explanation: The second sentence restates the result: the request was no longer being pursued.
questions.hint: Treat “in other words” as a paraphrase clue.

questions.statement: Read: “The display dimmed as the battery ran low. Icons became harder to see, though the device still worked.” What does “dimmed” mean?
questions.correctAnswer: Became less bright.
questions.explanation: The battery context and reduced visibility indicate lower brightness; the device did not stop working.
questions.hint: Use the visual consequence while keeping the contrast “though it still worked.”

questions.statement: A short note says: “The committee discussed a sanction after the review,” but does not describe the action or decision. What can be inferred about “sanction” from this note alone?
options: It proves that the committee punished someone.
It confirms that the committee approved the proposal.
It refers to a formal measure, but the note does not show whether it means approval or a penalty.
It means the review meeting was cancelled.
questions.correctAnswer: It refers to a formal measure, but the note does not show whether it means approval or a penalty.
questions.explanation: The noun “sanction” can refer to official approval or a penalty. The note gives no action or decision that distinguishes those meanings.
questions.hint: Identify what the note states, then check whether it gives a result that selects one sense.

questions.statement: A learner guesses that “reluctant” means “excited” in “She was reluctant to join; she asked to watch first.” Which check best tests the guess?
options: Replace it with “excited” again and ignore the second clause.
Choose a meaning because it looks like a Portuguese word.
Assume the writer made a mistake.
Replace it with “hesitant” and see whether the following action remains coherent.
questions.correctAnswer: Replace it with “hesitant” and see whether the following action remains coherent.
questions.explanation: “Hesitant” fits asking to watch first; “excited” conflicts with the stated behavior more strongly.
questions.hint: Test a near-synonym against the whole sentence.

questions.statement: A short message says, “The result was remarkable,” but gives no result, comparison or reaction. What is the best conclusion about “remarkable”?
options: It signals that the writer considers the result notable, but the reason and degree are not specified.
It proves the result broke a world record.
It means the result was exactly average.
It identifies which measurement was taken.
questions.correctAnswer: It signals that the writer considers the result notable, but the reason and degree are not specified.
questions.explanation: The adjective signals evaluation; without additional evidence, the specific reason for the judgment is unknown.
questions.hint: Separate the evaluation from facts the message does not provide.

questions.statement: Which sequence best supports a careful inference about an unfamiliar word?
options: Guess from spelling, then ignore conflicting details.
Identify its role, locate explicit clues, propose a meaning, test it in the whole sentence, and note uncertainty.
Translate each word separately and stop at the first meaning.
Choose the most technical definition whether or not it fits.
questions.correctAnswer: Identify its role, locate explicit clues, propose a meaning, test it in the whole sentence, and note uncertainty.
questions.explanation: The sequence combines grammar, textual evidence, a substitution test and a limit on certainty.
questions.hint: Look for a method that checks a hypothesis instead of stopping at a guess.

questions.statement: A passage includes “because,” “unlike” and “such as.” How can these words help infer vocabulary?
options: They guarantee that every unfamiliar word has one exact translation.
They signal cause, contrast and examples that constrain possible meanings.
They replace the need to read the surrounding sentence.
questions.correctAnswer: They signal cause, contrast and examples that constrain possible meanings.
questions.explanation: These connectors organize relations in the text; they provide clues but do not guarantee an exact translation.
questions.hint: Match each connector to the relation it signals.

questions.statement: Context suggests two possible meanings for an unfamiliar word, and both fit the paragraph. What is a useful next step?
options: Pick one meaning at random and report it as certain.
Ignore the paragraph and infer from spelling alone.
Check a suitable dictionary or a wider source and keep the ambiguity explicit until it is resolved.
questions.correctAnswer: Check a suitable dictionary or a wider source and keep the ambiguity explicit until it is resolved.
questions.explanation: When local clues do not distinguish meanings, a broader source can help. Until then, the evidence supports uncertainty.
questions.hint: Ask what additional evidence would separate the two meanings.
